claims.comparison_population: postmortem MS cases with low levels of meningeal inflammation and GM demyelination
claims.symptoms: high levels of meningeal inflammation and GM demyelination
claims.supporting_quote: Increased expression of proinflammatory cytokines (IFNγ, TNF, IL2, and IL22) and molecules related to sustained B-cell activity and lymphoid-neogenesis (CXCL13, CXCL10, LTα, IL6, and IL10) was detected in the meninges and CSF of postmortem MS cases with high levels of meningeal inflammation and GM demyelination.

claims.comparison_population: MS patients with lower levels of GM damage at diagnosis
claims.symptoms: higher levels of GM damage at diagnosis
claims.supporting_quote: Similar proinflammatory patterns, including increased levels of CXCL13, TNF, IFNγ, CXCL12, IL6, IL8, and IL10, together with high levels of BAFF, APRIL, LIGHT, TWEAK, sTNFR1, sCD163, MMP2, and pentraxin III, were detected in the CSF of MS patients with higher levels of GM damage at diagnosis.

claims.comparison_population: patients with MS and pathologically confirmed leptomeningeal inflammation
claims.supporting_quote: Moreover, we observed high CXCL13:BAFF ratios in post mortem cerebral spinal fluid from patients with MS and pathologically confirmed leptomeningeal inflammation, as well as in living patients with MS and radiologically confirmed paramagnetic rim lesions.

claims.comparison_population: patients with MS and radiologically confirmed paramagnetic rim lesions
claims.supporting_quote: Moreover, we observed high CXCL13:BAFF ratios in post mortem cerebral spinal fluid from patients with MS and pathologically confirmed leptomeningeal inflammation, as well as in living patients with MS and radiologically confirmed paramagnetic rim lesions.
Progressive MS patients had higher CSF cell counts, IgG-index, CHI3L1, MMP-9, CXCL13, NFL and MBP concentrations.

claims.symptoms: active disease according to consensus criteria
claims.supporting_quote: Active patients were younger and had higher NFL, CXCL13 and MMP-9 concentrations than inactive patients.

claims.comparison_population: neurosyphilis patients and Lyme neuroborreliosis patients
claims.supporting_quote: Median CXCL13 levels at baseline were 972 pg/mL for neurosyphilis patients, 8,000 pg/mL for LNB patients, and 7.8 pg/mL for MS patients. Patients with LNB and neurosyphilis showed significantly higher CXCL13 levels in their CSF compared to MS patients (p < 0.05, p < 0.001, respectively).

claims.comparison_population: NEDA group (no evidence of disease activity)
claims.symptoms: disease activity (relapses, new white matter lesions, EDSS change)
claims.supporting_quote: Forty-one patients experienced EDA and, compared to the NEDA group, had at diagnosis higher CSF levels of CXCL13, CXCL12, IFNγ, TNF, sCD163, LIGHT, and APRIL (p < 0.001).
CXCL13 was detectable in all samples and were higher in ON compared with healthy controls (HC) (p = 0.012).

claims.comparison_population: isolated optic neuritis (ION) patients and healthy controls
claims.symptoms: optic neuritis that progressed to multiple sclerosis (MS-ON)
claims.supporting_quote: In the TC, CSF levels in MS-ON were higher compared with ION patients and HC (p = 0.0001 and p<0.0001). In the VC, we confirmed the increase of CXCL13 in MS-ON compared to ION (p = 0.0091).
CXCL13 levels in the CSF discriminate ALS (n = 30) from Multiple Sclerosis (n = 16) patients with a sensitivity of 97.56%.
